chunks: ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:
"Any man whom the hadd punishment or qisas kills, then there is no diyah for him."
And he said: "Any man who attacks another man in order to strike him, and he repels him from himself and wounds him or kills him, then there is nothing upon him."
And he said: "Any man who looks in upon a people in their house in order to look at their private parts, and they throw at him and put out his eye or wound him, then there is no diyah for him."
And he said: "Whoever initiates aggression and is then retaliated against, there is no qawad for him."

key_terms.الْحَدُّ: the prescribed legal punishment established in the Sacred Law
key_terms.الْقِصَاصُ: retaliatory punishment in cases of unlawful killing or injury
key_terms.دِيَةَ: blood-money compensation owed for killing or bodily injury
key_terms.عَوْرَاتِهِمْ: their private parts or private matters that must not be exposed
key_terms.فَقَؤُوا: they put out or gouged out
key_terms.قَوَدَ: retaliatory execution or legal retaliation for killing

ai.seo_question: When is there no diyah or qisas liability in cases of killing or injury according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith states several legal rulings concerning cases in which no diyah or retaliatory liability is due. It covers death by lawful hadd punishment or qisas, self-defense against an aggressor, and injury to one who intrudes upon a household to look at private matters. The narration emphasizes that one who initiates unlawful aggression does not receive the normal protections accorded to a victim.
